body: Work on a building site outside Hyderabad has stopped for the middle of the afternoon, because in that heat there is nothing else it can do. The men are sitting along the north wall of a half-finished house in the strip of shade it throws, backs against the blockwork, and a boy has come round with water in a jerrycan and a steel tumbler that everybody drinks from and hands back. Nobody talks much. Over the next hour the shade narrows and moves and the whole row shuffles along the wall after it, without discussion, the way you move a chair. When the shade reaches the corner the row stands up.
Nobody on that wall thinks of shade as an image. It is a resource. It is rationed by the hour, it can run out, and a wall that throws it is worth more than a wall that does not.

Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths. The verse gets used constantly as an argument for tradition against novelty, and the tradition being defended is almost always a recent European one.

It is worth being exact about how recent. A hymnody a century and a half old. An order of service settled in the last few generations. An architecture, a dress code, an instrument, a way of standing at the front. Those things can be good and several of them are, but none of them is ancient, and the men on that wall in Hyderabad would find the Psalms describing their afternoon more precisely than any of them. The Lord is thy shade upon thy right hand is not a poetic flourish to a man who has just spent an hour following a shadow along a wall. It is a plain sentence about the difference between the sun and not the sun, and he had it before he opened the book.

This dial has a station built on exactly that observation. HM 313.80 — The Ancient Paths — carries Middle Eastern worship, and it sits inside an international block of 40 frequencies on a band running from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70.

Building a station on that principle is more expensive than building one that translates, and the reason is that translation is quick and formation is not. You can put a local text over an existing arrangement in an afternoon. Making music that assumes the room it is played in takes musicians who grew up in that room, and it takes a commitment to a frequency before anyone knows whether the frequency will be busy. Everything in the book happened in Asia, to Asians, in Asian languages, in a climate most Western church art has never depicted — and a band that believes that has to spend accordingly, or it is only saying it.

The reason this needs saying at all is that the picture got fixed a long time ago and then got printed. Centuries of European painting put the events in European rooms, in a northern light, on northern faces, in clothes nobody in the story ever wore. Those paintings went into books, the books went into Sunday schools, and the Sunday schools went everywhere the missionaries went. A child in Lahore learned the faith from an illustration of a man who looked nothing like anybody the child had ever met, and learned, underneath the lesson and without anybody intending it, that this was somebody else’s religion being lent out.

The band is arranged so that the lending stops. Each language holds one permanent frequency, hosted rather than dubbed, with its own presenters and its own catalogue, sitting in a regional block beside its neighbours. That arrangement carries a claim: a station in a language is not a version of the English one. It is the thing itself, in a place where the thing has been going on for a very long time.
And it changes what the recovery project actually is.

The standard word for this work is contextualisation, and the standard word is fair enough as far as it goes. It describes something real and useful — the labour of taking a text formed in one place and making it land in another, which is honest work that people have done carefully for generations. But the word carries an assumption in its pocket. It assumes the text is foreign and the context is local, and that the job is to move the first towards the second. Bride price. Honour and shame. Extended households under one roof, patronage, hospitality as an obligation rather than a kindness, land held by a family rather than a person. For a great many listeners those are not the local context. They are Tuesday.
The text was not written to be brought here. It was written here.

Late in the evening in Lahore a man carries a plastic chair out to the front of the house because it is still too warm to sit inside, and puts his phone on the window ledge with the station running low so as not to wake the children. The neighbour comes out for the same reason, leans on the low wall between the two houses, and listens to about half a song without saying anything. Then he asks what it is, because the melody wanders the way a ghazal wanders and comes back to its line the same way. The man says it is a psalm. The neighbour says he did not know they had those. They talk for a while about a water pump that has stopped working, and the station keeps playing behind the conversation, and neither of them turns it off.
Nothing in that exchange needed a translator, and nothing in it needed a bridge to be built. The song was already standing on the near side of the river.

There is a version of this argument that goes bad, and it should be named. It curdles into grievance — a running audit of what Europe took, a habit of reading every hymn for its passport, a Christianity that spends its energy on the question of who owns it. That version produces very little music and a great deal of resentment, and resentment is not one of the fruits. It is also ungrateful, because the translators, the grammarians and the printers who carried the text across the world did work that cost many of them their lives.

The point is not to take anything back from anybody. Nobody is being asked to give up a hymn, and a Welsh tune sung in Kerala is not a theft in either direction. The point is much smaller and much harder to unsee once you have seen it: that the oldest layer of this faith is Asian, and a listener in Chennai or Lahore is not standing at the far end of a supply chain. They are standing rather near the source, in a climate the text assumes, using categories the text uses without explaining them.

So the ancient paths are older than the argument they usually get used in. They are older than the hymnal, older than the organ, older than the countries that most of the arguments are had in. Ask for them and you are not asking for the nineteen-fifties. You are asking for a road that runs through heat and dust and shade, and it turns out that a good many people have been living on it the entire time and were never told that this counted.
All of which is a claim about the past until something is actually playing.

The dial carries four kinds of programming, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of the band — worship, gospel, hymns, country and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to leave running in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards, with more frequencies assigned and still in build behind the ones already on air.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 329.00 — Israel Inspire, the Hebrew-language station. Start there because this article has been arguing about origin, and that is where the argument bottoms out. Most of the book was written in that language, in that climate, by people describing the same sun and the same shade the men on the wall were following, and hearing worship in it does something no essay can do: it removes the layer of translation you did not know was there. You will not follow it. You will hear the consonants land where the poetry needs them to land, and you will notice that this is not a foreign language pretending to be scriptural. It is the other way round.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a correction. Put HM 329.00 on this evening while you are doing something ordinary — cooking, driving, sitting outside because the house is too warm — and do not concentrate on it. Let it be the thing playing behind a conversation about a broken pump. If somebody leans over the wall and asks what it is, you will have the whole of this article in one sentence, and you will not have to make any of the argument yourself.
